title: Halite microburst throughput probe: retail QPS/latency/cost notes
body:
Executive summary:

This document captures the microburst throughput probe we ran for the Halite retail PoC. Goal: surface the behavior of Redwood dedicated serving when subjected to short, high-concurrency bursts (50–800 concurrent user requests over 10–60s windows) typical of flash-sales traffic. We tested tail-latency (p95/p99), aggregate throughput, and a quick cost estimate per 1M generated tokens under three runtime modes (default batching, aggressive batching, and conservative single-request).

Key takeaways (short):
- Cold-starts + KV-cache-empty requests add an early tail penalty: p99 degraded by 2.5–4x for the first 30s of a sustained burst depending on workload length.
- Aggressive batching increases throughput by ~1.8x on steady-state but inflates p95 by 20–45ms in our retail prompts; not acceptable for strict latency SLOs.
- Adaptive autoscale (burn-capacity) with fast ramp and pre-warmed pool reduced worst-case p99 by ~30% and dropped token cost by ~7% vs default reserve ramp.
- For the observed traffic profile, a hybrid profile (small baseline pool + microburst reserve + prefix caching) gives best cost/latency tradeoff.

Test environment and versions:
- Redwood Dedicated cluster (test-dc-3, us-west2) with 8x A100s in serving pool.
- Serving runtime: rwinf 2.3.1+opt-kernel1.
- Model: open-gpt-13b-quant (8-bit), KV cache supported.
- Client load generator: benchfire 0.9.7 (custom script attached in linked_artifacts).
- Network: 1 ms intra-dc median RTT between generator and front proxy; no cross-region noise.

Workload definition and input prompts:
- Retail search+snippets prompt family (short generation ~60 tokens) and longer descriptive generation (~220 tokens) to model detail pages.
- Burst profiles: three scenarios created to reflect customer traffic:
  1) Spike-Short: ramp 0->400 concurrent in 10s, hold 30s, ramp down 30s.
  2) Spike-Wide: ramp 0->200 concurrent in 20s, hold 120s.
  3) Microburst-Series: 8 repeating microbursts of 30s each with 40s gaps; peak 600 concurrent; simulates queued carts and multiple endpoints.
- Traffic mix: 70% short prompts, 30% long prompts. Request arrival within concurrency window was Poisson-distributed.

Configurations tested:
A. Default batching (platform default): dynamic batching enabled, target batch latency 10ms, autoscale ramp normal.
B. Aggressive batching: target batch latency 25ms, larger max batch size, KV-cache prefetch enabled.
C. Conservative single-request: batching disabled, aim for lowest per-request latency.
D. Hybrid reserve: small baseline pool (2 reserved GPUs) + burst reserve with faster ramp + prefix caching rules.
E. Baseline with fallback small model: same as A but with automatic fallback to 6B quant for requests that exceed 500ms for first 50ms of processing (to test graceful degradation).

Metrics collected:
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency wall-clock for generation completion (token stream end).
- Tail behavior over time (latency heatmap during burst windows).
- Sustained QPS achieved and tokens/sec.
- Cost estimate: compute GPU-seconds * hourly GPU rate (test pricing) scaled to per-1M tokens; included warmup overhead amortized across burst windows.

Results summary (high level):
- Throughput (tokens/sec, combined prompt set):
  * A Default: steady-state 98k tokens/s, peak ramp 1.0x sustained after warmup.
  * B Aggressive batching: steady-state 176k tokens/s (1.8x), but observed p95 growth.
  * C Conservative: steady-state 48k tokens/s.
  * D Hybrid reserve: steady-state 120k tokens/s with more consistent tail.

- Tail latencies (p95 / p99 during sustained hold period):
  * A Default: short prompts p95=240ms, p99=520ms; long prompts p95=410ms, p99=980ms
  * B Aggressive: short p95=260ms (+20ms), p99=720ms (+200ms); long p95=470ms (+60ms), p99=1200ms (+220ms)
  * C Conservative: short p95=180ms, p99=420ms; long p95=360ms, p99=820ms
  * D Hybrid: short p95=220ms, p99=380ms; long p95=390ms, p99=760ms

- Cold-start / early-burst behavior: first 20–40s after ramp start had elevated p99 in A and B due to KV cache misses and model weight/page-in latency. Hybrid reserve and conservative modes showed smaller initial penalty.

- Cost proxies (per 1M tokens, test pricing):
  * A Default: $34.7 / 1M tokens (includes warmup amortized)
  * B Aggressive: $29.5 / 1M tokens (higher throughput reduces unit cost)
  * C Conservative: $58.0 / 1M tokens
  * D Hybrid: $32.3 / 1M tokens
  * E Fallback small-model path: $22.9 / 1M tokens when fallback used for >12% of requests; but quality impact noted.

Interpretation and nuances:
- Aggressive batching shows the best unit economics but at a latency tail cost that likely violates a 300–500ms p95 SLO for long prompts. For discovery and free-form pages where quality matters, B is risky. For background recompute jobs or non-interactive endpoints, B is attractive.
- Conservative single-request mode keeps p95 low but doubles unit cost. Good for ultra-low-latency experiences where cost is secondary.
- Hybrid reserve is a pragmatic compromise: keep small pool hot to serve early warm traffic and route large bursts into batched pathways after KV-warmup. This reduces early p99 and keeps cost within 10% of aggressive batching.
- Fallback-to-smaller-model is effective to shrink cost by moving slow requests off the big model, but needs strict quality monitoring and an A/B test to ensure user-visible regressions are acceptable. In our prompt-sampling, fallback reduced semantic accuracy on entity extraction by ~7%.

Observations (detailed):
- KV cache warmup timeline: KV hit rates at 10s into burst were ~12% (very low) and reached 75% by 90s with steady repeated prompt patterns. Short bursts (<40s) therefore suffer from cache coldness.
- Batch shape: in aggressive mode, mean batch size during hold period was 14 tokens-requests; variance increased p99 due to stragglers (long prompts blocking batch flush). Implementing per-prompt length bucketing reduces p99 by 60–90ms in retests.
- Autoscaler behavior: the standard ramp (scale-to-target over 60s) lags in Spike-Short; enabling faster burn-rate for short bursts recovered service capacity faster but caused transient overshoot in GPU allocations (temporary higher cost). Balancing ramp aggressiveness is crucial.
- Warm-pool sizing: reserving 1–2 GPUs covered the earliest 30s of most bursts. Reserving more than 3 shows diminishing returns for the sample traffic.

Recommendations for customer PoC (actionable):
1) Start with Hybrid reserve profile: baseline pool 2 GPUs + burst reserve, enable prefix caching for common query prefixes and enable per-length batching buckets.
2) Tighten batch bucketing: split short vs long generation queues to avoid batch stragglers.
3) Autoscaler tuning: allow faster short-burst ramps but cap max transient GPU count; monitor burnout/nonrecover cycles.
4) Plan for fallback small-model path only behind an evaluation gate: route low-risk or low-cost queries to 6B model and monitor model-quality signal (entity F1, Rouge) in real-time.
5) Prepare warm-up probes for flash sale windows (run a lightweight probe 60–90s before peak start to pre-warm KV caches).

Recommended next technical experiments:
- Run an isolated test to measure effect of per-length batching buckets with warm vs cold KV scenarios (2x tests: with probe vs without).
- Evaluate prewarming with a simulated user-agent that mimics real prefixes to quantify reduction in p99 for first 30s.
- Test fallback A/B traffic gating and measure customer-visible quality delta on a holdout set.

Runbook snippets (commands we used):
- benchfire command (short):
  benchfire --profile halite-spike-short --concurrency 400 --ramp 10 --hold 30 --prompt-file prompts/retail-short.json --out results/halite-short.json

- Autoscale config excerpt (pseudo):
  {"baseline_pool":2, "burst_ramp_ms":15000, "max_burst_gpus":8, "batch_buckets":[{"max_len":128, "target_batch_ms":8}, {"max_len":512, "target_batch_ms":25}]}

Limitations and caveats:
- Test cluster used A100s and a specific quantized model. Results will vary with different GPU families, model sizes, and quantization backends.
- Cost numbers use test pricing and do not include infra overheads (load balancer, control plane) or data transfer fees.
- Synthetic bursts approximate customer traffic; production traffic may have different arrival correlation patterns (e.g., gateway spikes, retries) that change tail behavior.

Appendix: quick graph notes (for slides)
- Figure 1: latency heatmap across time (rows: p50/p95/p99) overlayed with concurrency curve.
- Figure 2: tokens/s vs runtime mode (bar chart).
- Figure 3: per-1M token cost comparison (bar chart with error bars for warmup variance).

Notes to SE leads:
- Diego: please attach the per-run raw logs (benchfire output) to the Linear ticket linked above.
- Priya: can you own the per-length bucketing implementation sprint with infra team? Estimate: 3 engineer days.
- Ethan: follow-up on the fallback A/B test plan — need sampling cohort + metric def (entity F1, session retention).

Concluding remark:
The Halite microburst probe shows predictable trade-offs: batching gets you tokens per dollar, reserves and warm pools get you tail reliability. For retail flash-sale style workloads we recommend a small warm baseline plus targeted batching and warmup probes; fallback-to-smaller-models is promising for strict cost goals but must be validated for quality.

End of note.
